query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Al, Mn, or Si) high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent, and slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the nature of the X element. When X is Al, the preferential formation of a slow-growing, low-strain alumina (Al2O3) scale leads to a coherent barrier, whereas when X is Mn or Si, the resulting mixed oxide scales develop higher growth stresses and are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Alter the alloy composition by substituting X with Al, Mn, and Si, then expose the samples to sustained oxidizing or corrosive environments at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.conditions: Isothermal exposure in an oxidative atmosphere (e.g., air) or corrosive medium at temperatures above 900 °C for extended durations (e.g., 50–100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity, adherence, and growth behavior of the externally formed oxide scale, specifically the formation of a coherent and slow-growing alumina scale versus a mixed, crack-prone oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: In alloys with high Al content, the outward diffusion of Al leads to the formation of a continuous Al2O3 layer that grows slowly and has low volumetric mismatch, reducing internal stresses and preventing spallation. In contrast, when Mn or Si is the dominant reactive element, the resulting oxides are less mechanically compatible (via faster diffusion rates and greater expansion mismatches) and thus develop higher internal stresses that cause cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: CrFeCoNiAl alloys will form a steady, adherent, and protective Al2O3-dominated scale with slow mass gain, while CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi alloys will show faster-growing, non-coherent mixed oxide scales that crack and spall, leading to increased oxidation rates.
generation.baseline: The baseline is defined by CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is not optimized for protective oxide formation (e.g., Mn or Si), against which the beneficial effects of replacing X with Al are compared.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloy systems with controlled CrFeCoNi matrix compositions and X = Al, Mn, or Si, subjected to oxidizing or corrosive environments at temperatures exceeding 900 °C for long-duration exposures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise diffusion rates of the reactive species and the critical stress thresholds for scale spallation are not well quantified; additional microstructural factors may modulate oxide adhesion and long-term stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples with X = Al, Mn, and Si under identical processing conditions. Expose these samples to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at >900 °C under isothermal conditions for 50–100 hours. Characterize the oxide scales on each sample using SEM, XRD, and mass gain analysis.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (via SEM imaging)
Phase composition of the oxide scales (via XRD)
Mass gain over time to assess oxidation kinetics
Residual stress measurements in the oxide scales
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrFeCoNiAl sample does not demonstrate a slower-growing, more coherent, and adherent alumina-rich oxide scale (with lower mass gain and reduced crack formation) compared to the CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi samples under the identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Various stability criteria developed for high-entropy alloys are applied to compositions produced by mechanical alloying. While they agree with the annealed samples, these criteria fail to describe the as-milled metastable systems, highlighting the ability of mechanical alloying to overcome the limitations imposed by these criteria. The criteria are based on atomic size (Ω ≥ 1.1 and δr ≤ 6.6%) and/or electronegativity misfit, as well as on mixing enthalpy (Λ>0.95 J mol−1K−1 and −5 kJ mol−1<∆Hmix<0), or purely thermodynamic (ϕYe>20; ϕKing>1; Teff<500 K). These criteria are applied to several compositions found in the literature and to two metastable fcc solid solutions produced by mechanical alloying with compositions Al0.75CoXFeNi with X = Cr and Mn. Single-phase microstructures are stable up to above 600 K, leading to more stable multiphase systems after annealing above this temperature. Mössbauer spectrometry shows that, whereas the alloy with Cr is paramagnetic in the as-milled and annealed state, the alloy with Mn changes from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic behavior (Curie temperature ~700 K) after annealing. The fluctuation of the concentration of thermodynamically unstable oxide (Fe, Co, and Ni oxides) is higher than thermodynamically stable oxides (Al and Cr oxides), making the lines of Figure 5d–f appear thicker than Figure 5b,c. Similar observations can be made for all the oxide concentration plots, as well. As Fe, Co, and Ni oxides are thermodynamically unstable, the formation and dissociation occur more frequently in these oxides as compared to Al and Cr oxides.
